name: Mvog-Betsi Zoo
description: A zoo and primate rescue center home to gorillas, chimpanzees and other native wildlife, run in partnership with conservation groups.
history: Founded in 1951, the zoo originally served as a quarantine holding area for animals being exported out of Cameroon, before evolving into the wildlife park and botanical garden it is today. It's now managed by Cameroon's Ministry of Forestry and Wildlife.
fun_fact: The zoo's primates are cared for in partnership with Ape Action Africa, a conservation organization that began in the 1990s specifically to improve conditions for the primates living here.
travel_tips: Visit in the morning when animals are most active
Wear comfortable, closed shoes

name: Monument de la Réunification
description: A landmark monument commemorating the reunification of French and British Cameroon, with a spiral viewing platform over the city.
history: Commissioned by President Ahmadou Ahidjo, the monument was built between 1973 and 1976 by architect Armand Salomon, sculptor Gédéon Mpando, and Father Engelbert Mveng. It commemorates the 1961 reunification of French and British Cameroon, and later the 1972 formation of the United Republic of Cameroon.
fun_fact: The bronze sculpture in front of the spiral tower weighs 53 tonnes and stands 7 metres tall -- it depicts a man carrying four children, symbolizing the country's regions coming together as one nation.
travel_tips: A guided tour (where available) adds a lot of context
Photography rules can vary -- ask first

name: Notre-Dame des Victoires Cathedral
description: A striking Catholic cathedral known for its architecture and as a quiet spot in the busy city center.
history: The cathedral's distinctive triangular design was consecrated in 1955, making it one of the older landmarks still standing in what's now central Yaoundé.

name: National Museum of Yaoundé
description: Housed in a former presidential palace, showcasing Cameroonian art, artifacts and royal regalia.
image_attribution: Z. NGNOGUE, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
history: The building started life in the early 1900s as a residence during the German colonial period, later became the official presidential palace after independence, and was officially converted into Cameroon's National Museum in 1988.
fun_fact: Among the museum's roughly 30 rooms of artifacts is the saxophone once played by Manu Dibango, the Cameroonian musician known worldwide for the 1972 hit "Soul Makossa."
travel_tips: A guided tour (where available) adds a lot of context
